posts.title: Beyond Broadcast: Is the Media Industry Adapting Fast Enough?
posts.author: The Media Collective
posts.excerpt: The opening panel at OFF AIR 2026 explored the changing economics of television, the growing influence of digital platforms and whether the industry is making the right strategic choices to secure its future.
posts.body:
The transition from broadcast to IP may be one of the most significant technological shifts in television's history, but technology itself might be the least of the industry's problems.

At OFF AIR — The Unfiltered Future of Media, held at White City House in London on 24 November, Stuart Thompson, Editor of decodeTV, was joined by Gary Woolf of Constant Stream, Ian Nock of Fairmile West, Tuncay Pervaz of Tunpers Consulting and Xavier Leclercq of Broadpeak to examine the developments that have shaped the media industry in 2026.

What emerged was an industry confronting fundamental questions about its relationship with audiences, the economics of content and the sustainability of established business models.

## The end of broadcast is more than a technology transition

The debate surrounding the future of digital terrestrial television continues to focus on potential switch-off dates. But is the industry asking the right question?

Ian Nock argued that the transition towards internet-delivered television is fundamentally consumer-led. Audiences are already changing how they access content, and broadcasters must respond to those behaviours rather than attempt to preserve existing distribution models indefinitely.

Tuncay Pervaz offered a more cautious perspective, questioning whether the industry has sufficient evidence to ensure that the most vulnerable households will not be disadvantaged.

The distinction is important. Technical readiness does not necessarily equate to societal readiness.

Xavier Leclercq highlighted a further complication: the difference between the value television provides to an individual and the commercial value that individual represents to a broadcaster or advertiser.

For some people, television is a vital connection to the outside world. Yet those same viewers may not be particularly attractive to advertisers operating increasingly targeted, outcome-based campaigns.

If commercial incentives alone determine the pace of transition, the industry risks overlooking those who depend most heavily on its services.

The challenge is not simply delivering television over IP. It is managing a transition that remains commercially viable, socially inclusive and relevant to consumers.

## The YouTube dilemma

Few developments illustrate the industry's changing relationship with audiences more clearly than the rise of YouTube as a television platform.

Broadcasters that once sought to protect their content by keeping it away from third-party platforms are increasingly recognising that they need to be present wherever audiences choose to spend their time.

But that creates a strategic dilemma.

Distribution through YouTube offers access to audiences, particularly younger viewers, that traditional broadcasters may struggle to reach through their own services. It also places an important part of the relationship between content owner and consumer in the hands of another company.

Discoverability, advertising revenues and audience data are increasingly influenced by platform algorithms rather than the broadcaster.

Gary Woolf argued that making content discoverable across multiple platforms can strengthen programme recognition and introduce new audiences to established intellectual property. The challenge is ensuring that the content and its associated brands retain their identity in those environments.

Pervaz questioned the longer-term commercial implications of surrendering control of audience relationships, while Leclercq warned that bringing more high-quality broadcaster content to YouTube could further strengthen the platform's position.

For Nock, the issue extends beyond YouTube itself. Television is now competing within a finite pool of consumer attention, alongside gaming, social media and other forms of entertainment.

The question is no longer whether broadcasters should be on YouTube, but how they can participate in its ecosystem without undermining their own long-term commercial value.

## Can consolidation solve the industry's problems?

Against a backdrop of changing advertising revenues and increasing competition, consolidation has become a prominent feature of the media landscape.

However, becoming bigger does not necessarily mean becoming better.

Nock challenged the assumption that mergers and acquisitions provide an effective response to structural industry change. Consolidation may deliver efficiencies, but it does not automatically address declining audience relevance or a lack of innovation.

Woolf highlighted the implications for independent producers. As the number of major commissioners contracts and media organisations gain access to larger combined content libraries, opportunities for independent production businesses could become increasingly constrained.

Leclercq pointed to a similar dynamic within the technology supplier community. A shrinking pool of customers is likely to accelerate vendor consolidation, while encouraging a move towards broader, more integrated service offerings.

There was also recognition that collaboration, rather than consolidation alone, could play an increasingly important role in the future of content funding and distribution.

For broadcasters and suppliers alike, scale is only valuable if it creates the conditions for investment, innovation and sustainable growth.

## Is sports broadcasting becoming too fragmented?

Live sport remains one of television's most powerful differentiators. But the increasingly fragmented market for sports rights raises questions about whether the industry is serving fans effectively.

Woolf approached the issue from the perspective of a football supporter. Following a single team can require access to multiple broadcasters and streaming services, each with its own subscription.

While dividing rights packages may increase revenues for rights holders, it can make the overall experience more expensive and complicated for consumers.

Leclercq argued that excessive fragmentation risks encouraging piracy, potentially undermining the very revenues that rights holders are seeking to maximise.

Pervaz highlighted another challenge for streaming services: retaining subscribers once the sporting event or competition that attracted them is no longer available.

The acquisition of sports rights can be an effective customer acquisition strategy, but it does not necessarily deliver long-term customer loyalty.

Perhaps the industry needs to reconsider how it packages sport around the needs of fans, rather than exclusively around the requirements of rights holders and distribution platforms.

## AI: Commercial value before technological novelty

Artificial intelligence inevitably featured in the discussion, although the panel's focus was less on the transformative promises of AI and more on its practical commercial applications.

Woolf highlighted the opportunities for content owners to unlock value from extensive programme libraries through improved metadata, automated identification of relevant moments and the repurposing of existing content for different platforms.

Leclercq identified contextual advertising as an area of opportunity, using AI to identify appropriate moments within live content to introduce additional advertising inventory without unnecessarily interrupting the viewing experience.

Pervaz called for a more disciplined approach to technology investment, with innovation driven by identifiable business problems and measurable returns.

An audience intervention challenging the panel's assessment of AI-generated content, particularly in the rapidly developing microdrama market, demonstrated that the boundaries between automation, creativity and commercial opportunity remain far from settled.

The discussion reinforced an important distinction between what technology makes possible and what audiences actually value.

## Has sustainability fallen off the agenda?

One of the more revealing moments came towards the end of the discussion, when Leclercq expressed a desire to see sustainability return as an industry priority in 2027.

Nock acknowledged that sustainability had increasingly been overshadowed by the immediate commercial pressures facing broadcasters.

It is an uncomfortable reflection of the industry's current position. Organisations that are focused on protecting revenues, reducing costs and maintaining relevance may struggle to prioritise longer-term environmental objectives.

Yet decisions being made today about distribution infrastructure, cloud services and technology investment will have consequences for many years to come.

The challenge for 2027 will be to reconnect sustainability with commercial and operational decision-making, rather than treating it as a separate initiative.

## Four lessons for 2027

The panel concluded with four recommendations that captured much of the afternoon's discussion:

- Tuncay Pervaz: Use technology to solve genuine problems and assess the return on investment.
- Ian Nock: Diversify suppliers and avoid excessive dependency on individual providers.
- Xavier Leclercq: Put sustainability back on the industry agenda.
- Gary Woolf: Break down silos and embrace new forms of collaboration.

Together, they point towards an industry that needs to become more adaptable, commercially disciplined and open to alternative ways of working.

## Rethinking the business of television

Perhaps the most significant takeaway from The Debrief was that the media industry's challenges can no longer be considered in isolation.

Distribution influences discoverability. Discoverability influences audience relationships. Audience relationships influence advertising revenues and investment in content. And the economics of content ultimately determine the industry's ability to innovate.

Technology can help address many of these challenges, but it cannot compensate for a business model that no longer reflects how audiences behave.

As the industry looks towards 2027, its biggest challenge may not be keeping pace with technological change.

It may be having the confidence to challenge the assumptions on which its business has been built.

The Debrief was the opening panel at OFF AIR 2026 — The Unfiltered Future of Media, produced by The Media Collective, decodeTV and Faultline, with the support of Ateme, Appear, Norsk Video and Waldo Consulting.

This article is the first in a series exploring the discussions and insights from OFF AIR 2026.

posts.excerpt: How The Media Collective creates space for discussion, introductions and collaboration across media.
posts.body: The Media Collective brings together people across broadcast, studios, streaming platforms and technology partners. Our invitation-only gatherings are designed for senior leaders and decision-makers across media, entertainment and technology. Events take place at key moments in the industry calendar, with formats ranging from panel conversations and private screenings to informal evening receptions. Each gathering is curated for balance and relevance, creating space for thoughtful discussion, introductions and collaboration.
